hook.text: Two numbers from the same dashboard, on the same morning. Total signups: up again, the way they are every single day. Users still cooking four weeks after joining: down two points. Only one of them can tell you something is wrong.

plan.text: Product sense is that judgment, and there's no code in this round. The numbers in this video all come from one made-up recipe app. Eleven questions get a figure, and three close the round in a sentence each.

north-in.text: Begin with the number a whole team steers by.

north.text: Question one. What is a north-star metric, and what makes a good one? It's the single number that best captures the value users get, the one every team pushes toward.

north-good.text: A good one moves before revenue does, reflects real value, and is something the team's work can move. For this app: weekly cooks, people who open a recipe in cooking mode. Total signups is bigger, and says nothing about whether anyone cooks.

guard.text: Question two. What are guardrail metrics, and why do you need them? They're the health checks you refuse to harm on the way: crash rate, load time, unsubscribes, revenue. Almost any single number can be gamed. Send more notifications, and sessions climb while people quietly leave.

lead-in.text: Next, two ideas about proxies: when they move, and when they lie.

lead.text: Question three. Leading versus lagging indicators: why does the distinction matter? A leading indicator moves before the outcome, like cooking in the first week. A lagging one confirms it afterwards, like retention at month three.

lead-gap.text: Here an onboarding change lands in week three. Week-one cooking drops the next week. Month-three retention doesn't show it for twelve more. You steer by the leading line, as long as it actually causes the outcome, and isn't just correlated with it.

goodhart.text: Question four. What is Goodhart's law? When a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure. Reward support agents for closing tickets fast, and some close them before the problem is solved. Time to close falls from nine hours to three. Reopened tickets climb from four percent to fifteen. That second number is the counter-metric that catches it.

save-in.text: Now a question that hands you a feature.

save.text: Question five. How would you define success metrics for a Save for later button?

save-tree.text: Start from the job it does: bring people back to cook what they saved. So the primary metric is the share of saved recipes opened again within a week. Save rate and saves per user explain why it moved. Guardrails catch it stealing from the main flow: cooking sessions, and load time.

save-not.text: What you don't pick is clicks on the button. That measures the interaction, not the value.

drop-in.text: Then the question almost every loop includes.

drop.text: Question six. Walk me through diagnosing a sudden eight percent drop in daily active users, D A U. First: is it real? A logging change, a broken pipeline, or a holiday can make that shape on its own.

drop-split.text: Then, is it broad or narrow? Say the app had a hundred thousand daily users. Split by platform, iPhone and web barely moved. Android lost seventy-five hundred of the eight thousand.

drop-when.text: Then, what changed, and when? Android release five point two went out that morning. Last, internal or external: a competitor's launch looks different from a bug of your own.

noise.text: Question seven. How do you decide whether a change is signal or noise? Measure the normal swing first.

noise-band.text: This metric moves about three percent on an ordinary day, so a two percent dip sits well inside its band. In eight simulated weeks with nothing wrong, twenty-four days moved further than that.

noise-real.text: A real shift persists for days, clears the band, and shows up in related metrics too.

rec-in.text: Next, testing a change, and what to do when you can't.

rec.text: Question eight. How would you design an experiment for a new recommendation algorithm? Make it an A B test: users split at random between the old algorithm and the new one. State one primary metric, the share of users who cook a recommended recipe, with guardrails like latency and variety. And split by user, not by session, since one person's sessions aren't independent.

rec-size.text: Size it before launch. At a ten percent baseline, catching a lift to eleven takes about fifteen thousand users per group. Half that lift takes nearly four times as many. Then run whole weeks, so the weekends count.

cant.text: Question nine. When can't you run an A B test, and what do you do instead? When the change is global, like a redesign. When users affect each other, as in a marketplace. When there are too few of them, or when it would be unethical.

cant-instead.text: Then switch whole regions or time slots, or compare against a baseline: difference-in-differences, a synthetic control, an interrupted time series. Each trades some rigor for something you can actually run.

size-in.text: And last, the numbers you build on the spot.

market.text: Question ten. How would you estimate the size of something on the spot? Break it into factors, and say every assumption out loud. Daily searches for a new search-by-ingredient feature: two million monthly users, a quarter of them use it, half a session a day each, two searches a session. About five hundred thousand a day.

market-grade.text: The interviewer is grading the structure and the sanity check, not the number.

impact.text: Question eleven. How do you size a feature's impact before building it? Bound it. A hundred and twenty thousand weekly users reach the screen it lives on. Similar launches lifted cooking one to three percent. That's twelve hundred to thirty-six hundred extra weekly cooks, against a goal of twenty thousand.

impact-verdict.text: Even the best case is under a fifth of it. The cheapest experiment is the arithmetic.

rapid-in.text: Three left, each about a number you already have.

r-trade.text: When two metrics pull apart, name which is the goal and which is the limit. A notification change that lifts sessions five percent but raises unsubscribes two is only a win if the long-run math nets out positive.

r-vanity.text: A vanity metric looks good and only goes up, like total signups. Ask: if it doubled, would you know what to do differently? Prefer rates and cohorts, like week-four retention.

r-ratio.text: And a ratio can move because of its top, its bottom, or the mix underneath. Saves per user rose from two to two point four while saves fell, because a fifth of the users left. Read both halves, and add up counts across groups rather than averaging their ratios.

next.text: Every case in this round ends with someone pulling the numbers. In the next one, that's you, in Python. Next: Python and pandas.
